claims.text: Neural IR models are evaluated in narrow, in-domain settings that do not reflect zero-shot generalization
Prior multi-dataset IR benchmarks cover only a single task type or domain and do not test zero-shot generalization
BEIR contains 18 datasets across 9 retrieval tasks from diverse domains
BEIR evaluates 10 retrieval systems across five architecture families using nDCG@10
BM25 is a strong zero-shot baseline: it underperforms neural models 7-18 nDCG points in-domain (MS MARCO) yet outperforms many neural models in zero-shot settings
BM25+CE (cross-encoder reranking) achieves the best average zero-shot performance, +11% vs BM25, outperforming on 16/18 datasets
Dense models frequently underperform BM25: DPR -47.7%, ANCE -7.4%, TAS-B -2.8% on average
docT5query (document expansion) performs competitively: +1.6% vs BM25 on average, outperforming on 11/18 datasets
Re-ranking and late-interaction models have latency >350ms (GPU) versus dense models <20ms (GPU)
ColBERT requires ~900GB index for BioASQ (15M docs) vs BM25 18GB
Lexical methods have lower Hole@10 rates in TREC-COVID (BM25: 6.4%, docT5query: 2.8%) than dense models (TAS-B: 31.8%, ANCE: 14.4%)
After manually annotating 980 missing judgments in TREC-COVID, ANCE improves from 0.654 to 0.735, ColBERT from 0.677 to 0.735, while BM25 improves only from 0.656 to 0.668
TAS-B shows better zero-shot generalization than ANCE (outperforms on 14/18 datasets) and DPR (17/18 datasets) among dense models
Similarity function (cosine vs dot-product) affects document length preference and dataset-specific performance

limitations.text: All 18 datasets are English only; multilingual generalization is not tested
Annotation pools for several datasets were built with lexical systems, creating selection bias that underestimates non-lexical model performance
Document truncation at 512 word pieces disadvantages long-document retrieval; no error bars reported (models evaluated from fixed pre-trained checkpoints)
